A real raccoon in a city park.
Raccoons have a dark “mask” around their eyes and rings on their tails.
Their front paws work almost like hands, and they feel for food in the water.
They eat almost anything: fruit, bugs, fish, and sometimes trash!
Raccoons are most active at night.
This is Raccoon.
Marsh Rabbit
A real marsh rabbit at Sweetwater Wetlands Park in Gainesville, Florida.
Marsh rabbits live in Florida’s wet marshes and swamps.
Unlike most rabbits, they are good swimmers.
They often walk on their back legs instead of hopping.
They eat grasses and other plants.
This is Marsh Rabbit.
River Otter
A real river otter at a wildlife refuge.
River otters have thick fur that keeps them warm and dry in the water.
They can close their ears and nose when they dive.
They eat fish, crabs and crayfish.
Otters love to slide and play!
This is River Otter.
Burrowing Owl
A real burrowing owl standing on a post.
Burrowing owls live in holes in the ground instead of in trees.
They are awake during the day, not just at night.
They are small, only about 9 inches tall.
They bob their heads up and down when they are curious.
This is Burrowing Owl.
Florida Panther
A real Florida panther in Everglades National Park.
The Florida panther is Florida’s official state animal.
It is a kind of cougar, also called a puma or mountain lion.
Florida panthers are endangered. Only about 120 to 230 adults live in the wild.
They mostly hunt deer and wild hogs.
This is Florida Panther.
Key Deer
A real Key deer on Big Pine Key, Florida.
Key deer live only in the Florida Keys.
They are the smallest deer in North America, about as tall as a big dog.
They can swim from island to island.
They are endangered, so drivers go slowly where they live.
This is Key Deer.
Florida Black Bear
A real Florida black bear, photographed by a wildlife camera set up by Florida biologists.
The Florida black bear is Florida’s biggest land mammal.
Even though they are bears, they eat mostly plants, like berries, nuts and acorns.
They have an amazing sense of smell.
Locking up trash keeps bears safe and wild.
This is Florida Black Bear.
Loggerhead Sea Turtle
A real loggerhead sea turtle swimming overhead.
Loggerheads are named for their big, heavy heads and strong jaws.
They crunch crabs, clams and snails.
Mother turtles crawl onto Florida beaches at night to lay about 100 eggs.
Bright beach lights confuse baby turtles, so beach towns turn lights down at night.
This is Loggerhead Sea Turtle.
American Alligator
A real American alligator resting on the ground.
The American alligator is Florida’s official state reptile.
Alligators have a wide, U-shaped snout. Crocodiles have a pointier, V-shaped snout.
Their eyes and nostrils are on top of their head, so they can hide in water and still see and breathe.
Baby alligators chirp to call their mom.
This is American Alligator.
American Flamingo
A real American flamingo spotted at Clearwater Beach, Florida.
Flamingos get their pink color from the shrimp and algae they eat.
They often stand on one leg.
They eat with their heads upside down, filtering food out of the water with their beaks.
Wild flamingos are sometimes seen in Florida Bay and the Everglades.
This is American Flamingo.
Bottlenose Dolphin
A real bottlenose dolphin surfing the wave behind a boat.
Bottlenose dolphins are mammals, so they breathe air through a blowhole on top of their heads.
Each dolphin has its own signature whistle, a bit like a name.
They live in groups called pods.
They find food with echolocation: they send out clicks and listen for the echoes.
This is Bottlenose Dolphin.
